hints: Think of the general pattern when a reactive metal reacts with a dilute acid, what two types of product always form.
walkthrough:
Recall what metal plus acid gives**
You are with calcium, a Group 2 metal, plus dilute nitric acid. With dilute acids, reactive metals give a salt plus hydrogen. So here you get calcium nitrate plus hydrogen.

Balance the nitrate groups**
Calcium forms $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, so it needs two nitrate ions, $\text{NO}_3^-$, to make $\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2$. That means you need $2\text{HNO}_3$ on the left. The balanced equation is $$\text{Ca} + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2 + \text{H}_2$$

hints: Compare the solubility of calcium nitrate from (i) with calcium sulfate, which forms a solid crust.
Think about what that solid crust does to contact between fresh calcium surface and fresh acid.
walkthrough:
Picture what happens first**
At first calcium and dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ meet directly, so you get vigorous fizzing of $\text{H}_2$. The product $\text{CaSO}_4$ is sparingly soluble, unlike $\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ which is soluble.

See why the reaction blocks itself**
The insoluble $\text{CaSO}_4$ sticks to the metal as a solid crust. Think of it like paint coating the metal. Even though both calcium and acid are still present, the acid can no longer touch the clean metal underneath, so no more collisions occur and the reaction stops.

Final answer: $\text{CaSO}_4$ formed is insoluble and does not react further.
The $\text{CaSO}_4$ forms a coating / crust / protective layer on the calcium which prevents the sulfuric acid reaching the calcium surface, so reaction stops.

hints: Work out what charge calcium forms by losing its two outer 4s electrons, then recall its electronic structure.
walkthrough:
Find the cation**
Calcium is Group 2, electronic structure $2,8,8,2$. It loses its two outer electrons to form $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ with structure $2,8,8$.

Draw it correctly**
Draw Ca in the centre surrounded by 8 dots or crosses in the outer shell to show the full octet, with no electrons in the fourth shell, and put a $2+$ charge outside the brackets. Showing all electrons and the $2+$ charge earns the mark.
Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ showing 8 electrons in outer shell (2,8,8 arrangement) with $2+$ charge shown.

hints: Start from ethanedioic acid $(\text{CO}_2\text{H})_2$ and remove the two acidic $\text{H}$ atoms to leave the anion.
Remember how to show a displayed carboxylate group with a C=O double bond and a C-O- single bond plus the charge.
walkthrough:
Build from the acid**
Ethanedioic acid is $\text{HOOC}-\text{COOH}$. Remove both $\text{H}^+$ ions and you get the ethanedioate anion $^-\text{OOC}-\text{COO}^-$.

Show every bond**
In a displayed formula you draw every atom and every bond: $\text{O}=\text{C}-\text{O}^-$ joined by a C-C bond to the second identical unit. Put a single negative charge on each single bonded O, or a $2-$ overall, to show it is a doubly charged anion.

Final answer: Displayed structure $^-\text{O}-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{O}^-$ with all bonds shown.
Two $-$ charges on the carboxylate oxygens shown OR $2-$ overall charge shown.

hints: Recall what sodium chlorate(I), $\text{NaClO}$, is sold as in the supermarket for cleaning and whitening.
walkthrough:
Link to the familiar chemical**
$\text{NaClO}$ is household bleach. $\text{Ca}(\text{ClO})_2$ contains the same active $\text{ClO}^-$ ion, so it does the same job. It is used as bleach, a disinfectant or steriliser.
Final answer: bleach (or disinfectant / sterilising agent / killing bacteria)

hints: List the ions really reacting, $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{OH}^-$, and the two chlorine containing products $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{ClO}^-$.
walkthrough:
Write the ionic change**
Cold $\text{NaOH}$ provides $\text{OH}^-$. Chlorine is oxidised to $\text{ClO}^-$ and reduced to $\text{Cl}^-$ at the same time. Balance Cl, O and H and charge to get $$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}^- + \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Sodium ions are spectators, so they are left out of the ionic equation.

hints: Use O as -2 and total charge to solve for Cl in $\text{Cl}^-$ and in $\text{ClO}_3^-$.
walkthrough:
Apply the rules**
In $\text{Cl}^-$, Cl alone carries the charge, so $-1$. In $\text{ClO}_3^-$, let Cl be x: $$x + 3(-2) = -1$$ so $$x = +5$$ The given $\text{ClO}^-$ is $+1$, so the sequence is $+1 \rightarrow -1$ and $+5$.
Final answer: $\text{Cl}^-$ is $-1$ and $\text{ClO}_3^-$ is $+5$.

hints: Look at the oxidation numbers from (iii), +1 going both down to -1 and up to +5, and translate that into gain and loss of electrons.
walkthrough:
Translate oxidation number into electrons**
Going from $+1$ to $-1$ is a decrease, so gain of electrons (reduction). Going from $+1$ to $+5$ is an increase, so loss of electrons (oxidation). The same element does both, which is disproportionation described in electron terms.
Final answer: Chlorine both gains and loses electrons (is both oxidised and reduced).

hints: Recall the three products always formed when any carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate.
walkthrough:
Use the standard pattern**
Acid plus carbonate gives salt plus carbon dioxide plus water. Here the salt is calcium lactate, so the two other products you name are $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Final answer: carbon dioxide and water (plus calcium lactate)

hints: Identify reaction 1 as addition of HCN across the C=O of ethanal to make a cyanohydrin.
Recall the need for both HCN and a source of CN- such as NaCN or KCN for that addition.
Identify reaction 3 as oxidation of a primary alcohol $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to a carboxylic acid via an aldehyde.
Recall the strong oxidising mixture and heating method needed to get full oxidation to the acid.
walkthrough:
Sort out reaction 1**
Ethananal to 2-hydroxypropanenitrile adds H and CN across the $\text{C}=\text{O}$. You need $\text{HCN}$ plus a little $\text{NaCN}$ (or $\text{KCN}$) to provide $\text{CN}^-$ catalyst, usually cold.

Sort out reaction 3**
The reactant has $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, a primary alcohol, and the product has $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, a carboxylic acid. That is full oxidation. Use acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heated under reflux so no volatile aldehyde intermediate escapes before it is fully oxidised.

Final answer: Reaction 1: $\text{HCN}$ and $\text{NaCN}$ (or $\text{KCN}$).
Reaction 3: $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / $\text{H}^+$ / acid, heat under reflux.

hints: Think what happens when a -CN group is heated with aqueous acid to give -CO2H.
walkthrough:
Name the CN to acid change**
Reaction 2 converts $\text{CN}$ to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ using aqueous acid and water. Breaking by addition of water is hydrolysis, here acid hydrolysis of a nitrile.

hints: Look at reaction 4 where a ketone C=O becomes CH-OH, decide if hydrogen is added or removed.
walkthrough:
Spot the reduction**
In reaction 4 the keto group $\text{C}=\text{O}$ in pyruvic acid gains hydrogen to become $\text{CH}-\text{OH}$ in lactic acid. $\text{NaBH}_4$ supplies hydride, so it acts as a reducing agent.
Final answer: reducing agent (reductant / reduces)

hints: Look at the central C in lactic acid bonded to OH, H, CH3 and CO2H and state what makes that carbon chiral.
walkthrough:
Define the chiral centre**
Look at the middle carbon in lactic acid: it holds $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, four completely different groups. A chiral centre is a carbon with four different groups attached, giving non-superimposable mirror images.
Final answer: A carbon atom attached to four different groups / atoms.
